entities.name: Aurelian of Réôme
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aurelian of Réôme, a Frankish monk and scholar active in the mid-9th century, stands as a pivotal figure in the history of Western music theory, primarily known as the author of the *Musica disciplina*. Composed around 840 CE, this seminal treatise is the earliest comprehensive work on music theory to survive from medieval Europe, offering an invaluable window into the intellectual and practical understanding of music during the Carolingian Renaissance. His work systematically codified the eight church modes, fundamental to the structure of plainchant, thereby providing a theoretical bedrock for the liturgical music that permeated religious life across the Frankish Empire.

The *Musica disciplina* is not merely a theoretical exposition but also a pedagogical text, likely intended for the instruction of choir members and clergy in monastic centers. Aurelian meticulously details the characteristics of each mode, providing examples of liturgical chants that exemplify them. He draws upon earlier, fragmentary traditions and perhaps even lost Greek theories, synthesizing them into a coherent system applicable to Christian plainchant. This systematization was crucial for the Carolingian reform efforts aimed at standardizing liturgy and musical practice across Charlemagne's vast empire, ensuring uniformity in worship from Aquitaine to Saxony.

The enduring legacy of Aurelian's *Musica disciplina* lies in its foundational role for subsequent generations of medieval music theorists. His definitions and classifications of the modes became standard, influencing figures like Hucbald, Guido of Arezzo, and beyond. By providing a clear, written framework for understanding and performing plainchant, Aurelian facilitated the transmission of musical knowledge and practice at a time when oral tradition still dominated much of cultural life. His work thus not only preserved but actively shaped the development of Western sacred music for centuries.
